title: Bessel Functions in Synthesis — rich
forward_vector: I am the manifest of Bessel Functions in Synthesis's rich face, its first round, a Sketch made in the proposal round of 2026-11: the two proofs of 2026-05-04 gathered beside the sections they drew, and three made walks, each opening on one idea and ending on its section's claim, tested: the carrier null at the first zero of J0 with the sideband ladder against a printed table, a string against a round drum head struck anywhere, and the Bessel function played as the sound with its order as a knob. I hold the fingerprint of the words each was laid against, and the offers the making found for the text. I grow when Loudon has heard the null and answered the offers; I never hold the entry's words.

offers.what: The 1:1 sentence: "Why does FM with ratio 1:1 sound like a buzzy sawtooth? Because the sideband amplitudes follow J₀(β), J₁(β), J₂(β)…" At 1:1 every partial does land on a harmonic, as a sawtooth's do. But the lower sidebands fold past 0 Hz onto the upper ones, so the k-th harmonic is J₍ₖ₋₁₎(β) + (−1)ᵏ J₍ₖ₊₁₎(β), not one Bessel value. The carrier piece measures it. At 1:1 and β 2.4048 the 220 Hz partial is J₀ − J₂ = −0.432 (−7.3 dB), not silent. And at no index from 0.2 to 8 do the first ten harmonics come within 15 dB of a sawtooth's 1/k: the closest is 15.1 dB, at β 6.78. Suggested: "At 1:1 the sidebands fall on every harmonic, as a sawtooth's do, but each harmonic is two Bessel values, the upper sideband's and a lower one folded back, so the slope is not a sawtooth's; the sawtooth FM is known for comes from feedback ([[FM Synthesis]] § Feedback)."

"This is not an approximation" holds, and the piece shows it at its sharpest. At β 2.4048 the carrier, measured from the engine's own samples, is 241 dB down. Every sideband from −7 to +7 sits on |Jₙ(β)| to under 0.001 dB across β 0 to 6. The ladder above the carrier matches a printed table at β 1, 2 and 5 to ten places. The clause it lacks is where the exactness lives. Suggested, after "exact solution": "for a sine modulator, sideband by sideband. A partial you hear is a single Jₙ only when no other sideband lands on it; at low ratios, sidebands below 0 Hz fold back and add."

offers.section: Synthesis Applications from Direct Bessel Waveforms
offers.what: "The peak of Jₙ occurs approximately at t=n": the order does set the peak, later for every higher n, as the section says. But the peak comes after n, not at it, and the gap grows. The first peaks are at 1.841, 3.054, 4.201, 5.318, 6.416, 7.501, 8.578 and 9.647 for n = 1 to 8, which is 0.84 to 1.65 later, following n + 0.81·n^⅓ to within 0.04. What happens near t = n is the waking: Jₙ is nearly silent before it and already about 70 % of its peak at it. Suggested: "Jₙ stays near silent until about t = n, then peaks a little after, near n + 0.81·n^⅓ (1.84, 3.05, 4.20 for n = 1, 2, 3)."

offers.section: Synthesis Applications from Direct Bessel Waveforms
offers.what: "Non-uniform zero-crossing spacing", and in the LFO paragraph "the irregular oscillation rate (slowing as amplitude decays)". J₀'s zeros, found by the piece, are 2.405, 5.520, 8.654, 11.792, so the gaps are 2.405, 3.115, 3.134, 3.138, 3.139. Only the first is uneven. After it every gap is within 1 % of π and closer each time, so the slowing is real but under 1 %. Past x = 5, J₀ differs from a plain cosine an eighth of a turn late, fading as 1 ⁄ √x, by at most 0.0077. What sets J₀ apart from a sine is that fade, and its start at full height, not the spacing of its zeros. Suggested: "zero-crossings that start uneven and settle quickly to an even spacing of π, under an amplitude that fades as one over the square root of time."

The same finding, in this section's words: "The zero-crossings are irregularly spaced (roots at approximately 2.4, 5.5, 8.65...), creating a unique temporal signature that no simple sinusoid can produce." The roots are right. The irregularity is only the first gap (2.405, then 3.115, 3.134, 3.138 → π), and a sine an eighth of a turn late, fading as 1 ⁄ √t, follows J₀ to within 0.0077 past x = 5. The order piece in the next section plays the two side by side. Suggested: "(roots at about 2.4, 5.5, 8.65 …, spaced ever closer to π): a ring that starts at full height and fades as one over the square root of time, close to a decaying sine but for its first moments."

Not tested by a piece; the drum head piece tests only the membrane, and these numbers were computed in scratch with SciPy. "The first few modes of a struck gong or tam-tam are not at simple integer ratios—they follow the Bessel zero spacing" holds for a membrane, a drum head, and not for a gong or tam-tam, which is a plate. A plate's modes are built from Jₘ and the modified Iₘ together, and its frequencies go as the square of a different root. A clamped round plate runs 1 : 2.08 : 3.41 : 3.89 (roots 3.196, 4.611, 5.906, 6.306), against the membrane's 1 : 1.59 : 2.14 : 2.30. A free-edged plate, nearer a gong, follows another series again (Fletcher and Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, ch. 3). A church bell is a shell, and founders tune it toward hum, prime, tierce, quint and nominal near 0.5 : 1 : 1.2 : 1.5 : 2. So the membrane sentence holds, and the gong, tam-tam and bell sentences want "plate" or "shell", where the modes are still circular, Bessel-built and inharmonic, but not at the Bessel-zero spacing. The same holds for Pedagogical Revelation's "You cannot make a circular bell that rings like a harmonic sine wave": founders do get near it, by shaping the profile.

pieces.title: J₀ to J₆ against β, and the FM spectrum at β 2, 4 and 6
pieces.caption: The curves above, the spectra they predict below, at 1000 and 200 Hz. A record of the maths, drawn from Jₙ itself, not measured from a sound; the piece beneath measures. At β 6 the lowest stem it draws, J₅ at 0 Hz, is one the ear would never hear: a sine at 0 Hz is nothing.

pieces.title: The carrier null · is it exactly Jₙ?
pieces.caption: **One FM pair at 11 : 1, the index walked from 0 to the first zero of J₀.** It opens on the carrier alone, adds the first pair, then the whole family of Jₙ curves, then a narrow window that lets you hear the carrier by itself, and ends on the section's claim at its sharpest point. It holds: at β 2.4048 the carrier, measured from the engine's own samples, is 241 dB down, gone, and through the window the sound drops 55 dB. Every sideband from −7 to +7 sits on |Jₙ(β)| to under 0.001 dB from β 0 to 6, and the ladder above the carrier matches a printed table at β 1, 2 and 5 to its ten places. The last control tries 1 : 1, the ratio the section names for the sawtooth, and there the carrier does not vanish: J₂'s lower sideband folds onto it, and what you hear is J₀ − J₂ = −0.432.

pieces.title: the first six modes of a round drum head
pieces.caption: Each mode's shape, Jₘ(j r) cos(mθ), with its zero: (0,1) at 2.40, (1,1) 3.83, (2,1) 5.14, (0,2) 5.52, (3,1) 6.38, (1,2) 7.02. Red and blue move opposite ways; the white lines between are still.

pieces.title: A string and a drum head · who decides the partials?
pieces.caption: **A string and an ideal round drum head at the same 140 Hz, struck.** It opens on the string, whose partials sit on whole numbers wherever you strike it; then the drum head, whose partials fall at Bessel zeros the piece finds for itself (they match the printed table to four places); then the two side by side; and ends on the section's claim where it would break: strike the drum anywhere. The strike chooses which modes sound, the centre leaving only the rings at 1, 2.295, 3.598, 4.903, but never where they are. Of 99 strike radii, the best puts 8.5 % of the overtone power within 20 cents of a whole number; the string puts all of it there. An ideal membrane, with no air: a real kettle drum's air pulls its modes toward a pitch.

pieces.title: The order as a knob · when does Jₙ arrive?
pieces.caption: **The Bessel function played as the sound itself, then slowed to a swell so its timing is heard.** It opens on J₀ alone, holds it against its shadow (a cosine an eighth of a turn late, fading as 1 ⁄ √t), wakes J₁, turns the order smoothly from 0 to 8, and ends on this paragraph's claim about the peak. The section's numbers hold for J₀'s zeros (2.405, 5.520, 8.654) and J₁'s peak (1.841). The zero spacing is uneven only at the start: after the first gap, every gap is within 1 % of π. And the peak of Jₙ is not at t = n but later, 0.84 at n = 1 and 1.65 at n = 8, following n + 0.81 · n^⅓; near t = n it is waking, already about 70 % of the way up.
